sections.h2: What is a small estate affidavit in Illinois?
sections.html:
It is a sworn statement that lets a person holding a dead person's money or property release it to the heirs without a court case. Section 25-1 of the Probate Act of 1975, 755 ILCS 5/25-1, tells a bank, a transfer agent or anyone owing the decedent money to pay or deliver to the people named in a conforming affidavit. The holder who acts in good faith on a copy that substantially follows the statutory form is protected as if the payment had gone to a court appointed representative.

The key phrase for homeowners is "personal property." The affidavit covers cash, accounts, safe deposit contents and similar items, and it does not cover the house.

sections.h2: What is the Illinois small estate affidavit limit?
sections.html:
The limit is $150,000 in tangible and intangible personal property, not counting motor vehicles registered with the Secretary of State. That figure comes from Public Act 104-346, effective August 15, 2025, and applies to a decedent who died on or after that date. A second amendment, Public Act 104-624, takes effect January 1, 2027 and leaves the $150,000 figure alone while listing vehicle types that no longer count as excluded vehicles.

Source: 755 ILCS 5/25-1, subsection (a-5).

If the affidavit is used only to retitle vehicles with the Secretary of State, it can transfer them without regard to the value of the personal estate.

sections.h2: Can an Illinois small estate affidavit transfer a house?
sections.html:
No. The statute speaks of transferring personal property, and Illinois Legal Aid Online says plainly that the affidavit cannot be used to transfer real property such as a house. It adds that the decedent's real estate may already have passed by a Transfer on Death Instrument or by joint tenancy, in which case the affidavit can still handle the rest of the estate.

When the house is titled in the decedent's name alone, the usual route runs through the circuit court. Under 755 ILCS 5/20-1, a representative appointed by the court takes possession of the decedent's real estate during administration, collects rents, keeps the buildings in repair, pays taxes and liens and may insure the property. Subsection (d) leaves intact the representative's power to sell or mortgage real estate under the Probate Act.

sections.h2: What conditions must be met before using the affidavit?
sections.html:
Subsection (a-5) sets two gates. No letters of office can be outstanding on the estate, and no petition for letters can be contemplated or pending in Illinois or any other jurisdiction. The decedent's personal estate passing by intestacy or under a will must stay within the dollar limit. The affiant also attaches a copy of the death certificate, and a certified copy of the will if one was filed.

A person who holds a will must file it with the clerk of the proper county right after the testator dies, under 755 ILCS 5/6-1. Hiding a will for 30 days after learning of the death is sentenced as a Class 3 felony. The affidavit is signed before a notary under penalty of perjury, and an out of state affiant names an Illinois agent for service of process.

Illinois Legal Aid Online says the form can be downloaded from the Secretary of State's website or picked up at the circuit clerk's office, and it suggests making at least two copies of the signed affidavit to show to each bank or company holding property of the estate. A holder who refuses to turn the property over can be taken to civil court.

Items the affidavit must list include:

  • The affiant's addresses and relationship to the decedent
  • The decedent's name, date of death and last residence
  • Each asset with its fair market value and every registered vehicle
  • Known unpaid debts by class, or a statement that all debts were paid
  • The surviving spouse, minor children and adult dependent children
  • The heirs or legatees and each share

sections.h2: Who gets paid first from an Illinois small estate?
sections.html:
Creditors come before heirs. Paragraph 7.5 of the affidavit says every valid claim must be paid from the estate before anything goes to an heir or legatee, and if a class cannot be paid in full, its claims are paid pro rata. The affiant also agrees to indemnify creditors, heirs and anyone relying on the affidavit for losses caused by the affiant's act or omission, with attorney's fees owed to a person who recovers.

The statutory order of classes is:

  • Class 1: funeral and burial expenses, administration expenses and statutory custodial claims
  • Class 2: the surviving spouse's or child's award
  • Class 3: debts due the United States
  • Class 4: wages owed employees, up to $800 per claimant, for services within 4 months before death, and last illness expenses
  • Class 5: money or property held in trust that cannot be identified or traced
  • Class 6: debts due the State of Illinois and local governments in Illinois
  • Class 7: all other claims

The award for a surviving spouse who was an Illinois resident is $20,000 plus $10,000 for each minor or adult dependent child who lived with the spouse at the time of death. With no spouse, the same amount goes to those children in equal shares.

sections.h2: How does selling an inherited Illinois home work when the affidavit does not apply?
sections.html:
The seller needs legal authority first. If the home is in the decedent's name alone, an heir cannot sign a deed on the strength of an affidavit, so the sale waits for a court appointed representative or another transfer of title. Ask the clerk of the circuit court in the county where the decedent lived what filings the probate division requires, and ask the county recorder what proof of authority it expects with a deed.

Under section 20-1, a representative may not take possession of the portion of real estate occupied as a residence by the heir or legatee unless the will says so or the court finds possession is necessary for claims, administration costs, taxes, preservation or distribution. The court may also hand possession to an heir or legatee on petition if the property will not be needed to pay debts.

The affidavit can still handle bank accounts and vehicles while the house moves through probate, which keeps the two tracks separate. Taxes, insurance and upkeep on the house continue in the meantime, and the representative carries those duties.

faqs.q: What is the small estate limit in Illinois?
faqs.a: $150,000 in personal property, not counting motor vehicles registered with the Secretary of State, under 755 ILCS 5/25-1 as amended by Public Act 104-346.

faqs.q: Can I sell my parent's house with a small estate affidavit?
faqs.a: No. The affidavit transfers personal property only. A house titled in the decedent's name usually needs a court appointed representative before it can be sold, unless it already passed by a Transfer on Death Instrument or joint tenancy.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay the decedent's debts before giving heirs their share?
faqs.a: Yes. The affiant must pay valid claims in the statutory order before any distribution to an heir or legatee, and signs an indemnity for losses caused by the affiant's acts or omissions.

faqs.q: How much is the spouse or child award in an Illinois small estate?
faqs.a: $20,000 for the surviving spouse plus $10,000 for each minor or adult dependent child who lived with the spouse at death. With no spouse, that sum is divided equally among the children.

faqs.q: Does a small estate affidavit need a notary?
faqs.a: Yes. The form is signed and sworn before a notary public under penalty of perjury, and a fraudulent statement is perjury under section 32-2 of the Criminal Code of 2012.
